records.title: Record 2023 Caribbean marine heatwave began one to two months early and was followed by coral die-offs across the wider Caribbean
records.description: NOAA and University of Queensland scientists reported in December 2023 that extreme marine heatwaves covered the wider Caribbean, with record heat stress that started one to two months earlier than usual and lasted longer. A 2024 field study reported abnormal heat of 1 to 3 C above normal from March 2023, lasting more than five months in parts of the region, and a May 2026 study found most surveyed Caribbean sites had tipped into net reef erosion.

location.name: Wider Caribbean Sea (regional)
location.detail: Wider Caribbean including Florida-adjacent waters; longest heat stress reported around Jamaica, Haiti, Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica (ref 3)

records.layer_rationale: A basin-scale sea-surface heat anomaly is a physical climate event, with reef damage as its downstream effect.

notes.harm: NOAA's Coral Reef Watch coordinator said high mortality of staghorn and elkhorn corals had been reported in Florida, Puerto Rico and Mexico, and a study reported 60 to 100% of reef bleached in some areas with many patches dead (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: None of the opened sources reports a fishery, tourism or port restriction tied to the 2023 heatwave itself (refs 1-5).
notes.scale: NOAA said nearly all reef regions in the wider Caribbean were exposed to about double the heat stress expected to cause mortality, a regional-sea extent (ref 1).
notes.duration: Abnormal heat lasted more than five months in parts of Haiti, Jamaica, Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica, the longest on record there, which is months rather than a year (ref 3).
notes.significance: The finding rests on NOAA's report with the University of Queensland and Coral Reef Watch heat-stress products, which is an agency notice but no enforcement or declaration (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: NOAA: nearly all coral reef regions in the wider Caribbean, including Florida, were exposed to about double the heat stress expected to cause mortality (ref 1).

records.title: May to late-autumn 2023 ocean heat wave bleached reefs along Belize's barrier reef tract
records.description: A marine heat wave that began in May 2023 pushed water temperatures to about 32 C and kept them high until late autumn along an almost 200-mile stretch of Belize's barrier reefs and atolls. Belize's Fisheries Department confirmed bleaching in late June 2023 and ran monitoring surveys in marine reserves through November 2023.

location.name: Belize Barrier Reef tract
location.detail: Almost 200-mile stretch of barrier reefs and atolls off Belize, including Hol Chan, Glover's Reef and Turneffe Atoll marine reserves (refs 1, 2)

records.layer_rationale: The finding is a sustained sea-temperature anomaly, with bleaching as its observed effect.

notes.harm: Woods Hole's Oceanus reported that in some areas all coral colonies were stark white and described widespread loss in coral cover throughout Belize, without a measured percentage (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The opened sources report no closure or restriction on fishing or tourism tied to the heat wave (refs 1-3).
notes.scale: The heat wave covered an almost 200-mile (321 km) tract of reefs and atolls, which is a national coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: Temperatures of about 32 C persisted from May until late fall 2023, about six months, and the Fisheries Department surveyed in September to November 2023 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: NOAA Coral Reef Watch issued a Bleaching Alert Level 2 for Belize and the Fisheries Department confirmed bleaching in June 2023 and the National Coral Reef Monitoring Network surveyed eight marine reserves and one national park (ref 2).

records.title: Hurricane Beryl's storm surge and winds devastated Carriacou, Petite Martinique and the Grenadines in July 2024
records.description: Beryl struck Carriacou as a Category 4 hurricane on 1 July 2024. The US National Hurricane Center says its track caused severe storm surge impacts in Grenada and its dependencies and in St. Vincent and the Grenadines, where no surge observations exist. Grenada's Meteorological Service reported 99% of buildings on Carriacou damaged or destroyed, and the NHC puts damage at USD 218 million for Grenada and USD 231 million for St. Vincent and the Grenadines.

records.layer_rationale: Storm surge is a physical coastal flooding hazard driven by a hurricane.

notes.harm: The NHC attributes 3 direct deaths in Grenada and 8 in St. Vincent and the Grenadines to Beryl, with wind, surge and collapsed structures combined and no surge-only breakdown (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Grenada's Meteorological Service reported 99% of Carriacou buildings and 70% of Petite Martinique buildings damaged or destroyed, including Carriacou's only hospital (ref 1).
notes.scale: Severe surge impacts are reported across two countries' island groups, a national-coastline extent rather than a single site (ref 1).
notes.duration: The landfall on Carriacou was at 1520 UTC on 1 July 2024 and the surge was a one-day event (ref 1).
notes.significance: The NHC's official Tropical Cyclone Report documents the impacts, and Grenada's prime minister described the surge as extensive (refs 1, 2); no separate order is cited.

records.title: Hurricane Melissa's storm surge destroyed Black River and the southwest coast of Jamaica in October 2025
records.description: Melissa made landfall in western Jamaica as a Category 5 hurricane on 28 October 2025. The National Hurricane Center estimates surge of 7 to 11 ft above ground near Crawford and Black River with large destructive waves, and Jamaican officials cited up to 13 ft. The NHC reports 45 deaths in Jamaica and a World Bank damage estimate of USD 12.2 billion, 41% of 2024 GDP.

records.title: Cartagena builds a 250,000-million-peso coastal protection scheme against erosion and flooding as Bocagrande faces rising seas
records.description: Colombia's disaster agency UNGRD and Cartagena's mayor's office are building a coastal protection megaproject in Bocagrande with groynes, breakwaters, seawalls, drainage and new beaches, costing about 250,000 million pesos, 62% paid by the national government. The city's Plan 4C projects sea level rise of 15 to 20 cm by 2040 putting more than 80% of neighbourhoods at risk without adaptation, and a 2019 study modelled up to 97.2% of Bocagrande flooded by 2100.

notes.significance: The national government funds 62% of the programme and the city's Plan 4C is a formal adaptation plan with the 2040 sea-level projection (ref 1).

records.title: Caribbean surface waters are acidifying, with aragonite saturation falling at La Parguera and the only Caribbean time series left sparse
records.description: A 2025 Frontiers in Marine Science paper reports Caribbean surface aragonite saturation has declined by about 3% since pre-industrial levels and surface acidity rose roughly 10% from 1992 to 2015. La Parguera, Puerto Rico, hosts the only sustained CO2 time series, the CARIACO series off Venezuela was discontinued in 2017, and a Puerto Rico assessment finds aragonite saturation there falling 0.098 units per decade.

records.layer_rationale: Falling seawater pH and aragonite saturation are a chemical-physical change driven by atmospheric CO2.

notes.harm: The papers report falling aragonite saturation, with La Parguera waters below the 3.7 carbonate-sediment dissolution threshold for up to 90% of the year, but no direct organism loss is documented (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: No fishery, shellfish or tourism restriction linked to acidification appears in the opened sources (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The trend is described for the wider Caribbean, a regional sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: Aragonite saturation at La Parguera has declined by 0.098 units per decade in monitoring since 2009 and surface acidity rose 10% over 1992-2015, so chronic (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The sources are a peer-reviewed paper and a research framework; no regulator action or standard breach is cited, though SDG 14.3.1 reporting is mentioned (ref 1).

records.description: NOAA-supported summer cruises led by LUMCON measured the bottom-water low-oxygen zone off Louisiana and Texas at about 6,705 square miles in July 2024, 4,402 in July 2025 and 1,332 in July 2026. records.title: Louisiana cancels the Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion after permit suspension, leaving land loss unaddressed
records.description: The Mid-Barataria Sediment Diversion, intended to divert Mississippi River water and sediment into the Barataria Basin and build land, was cancelled on July 17, 2025, announced by Louisiana's coastal authority and the Louisiana Trustee Implementation Group, after the Army Corps suspended its permit. More than $600 million had been spent without completing the project; the basin has lost roughly 432 square miles of land since 1932 and the state has pivoted to a smaller diversion at Myrtle Grove.

location.name: Barataria Basin and Barataria Bay
location.detail: Southeast Louisiana, Jefferson and Plaquemines parishes; the diversion was designed to divert up to 75,000 cubic feet of river water per second.

records.layer_rationale: A government decision to end a coastal restoration project amid permitting, cost and fisheries disputes.

notes.harm: The basin has lost roughly 432 square miles of land since 1932 per ASCE, and the 2022 EIS projected up to about 17,300 acres of new land by 2050 that will not be built (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: Oyster and brown shrimp concerns drove opposition, but no fishery closure from the diversion is documented, since it was never completed (refs 1, 3).
notes.scale: The cancellation concerns one basin project, while the land loss it targeted is basin-scale along coastal Louisiana (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Land loss has run since 1932 and the project spanned construction from August 2023 to cancellation in July 2025 (ref 2).
notes.significance: The Army Corps suspended the project's permit and the trustees cut the authorized budget from $2.26 billion to $618.52 million on July 17, 2025 (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure appears in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The authorized budget was reduced from $2.26 billion to $618.52 million, reflecting funds already spent, as the project was cancelled on July 17, 2025 (Louisiana Trustee Implementation Group, as reported by Fox 8).

records.title: Crude oil spill from Dos Bocas marine terminal fouls Tabasco beaches and halts fishing in May 2025
records.description: From May 4, 2025 residents and fishermen in Paraíso, Tabasco reported tar and crude on beaches near Mexico's Dos Bocas marine terminal, with beaches closed along nearly 17 km of coast, fish deaths reported and fishing paralyzed. Mexico's environmental safety regulator ASEA confirmed the spill came from the Dos Bocas marine terminal and asked Pemex for a detailed report on its causes; oil also reached mangroves and the Mecoacán lagoon, per local reports.

location.name: Dos Bocas marine terminal and Paraíso coast
location.detail: Paraíso, Tabasco, southern Gulf of Mexico (Bay of Campeche), next to the Olmeca (Dos Bocas) refinery; Spanish-language sources.

records.layer_rationale: Hydrocarbon release from a marine oil terminal contaminating coast, mangroves and fisheries.

notes.harm: Residents reported dead sábalo, jurel and bonito and effects on oyster larvae and pelicans, and tar reached mangroves and the Mecoacán lagoon, but findings by authorities were not found (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Public beaches were closed for nearly 17 km of coast and fishing was paralyzed, per local reports (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The affected stretch is one coastal municipality's shoreline and an adjoining lagoon (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The reports describe the first days after May 4, 2025, and no later duration is documented in the pages opened (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: ASEA, an agency of Mexico's environment ministry, began a supervision of Pemex and requested a detailed report on causes (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Corpus Christi Ship Channel deepening for supertankers would dredge 46 million cubic yards into the Gulf
records.description: The Port of Corpus Christi Authority has applied to deepen the ship channel from 54 to about 75 feet so fully laden very large crude carriers can load, extending the entrance channel into the Gulf (a roughly 10-mile extension in the draft EIS; the Corps' 2019 notice described 13.8 miles of deepening); the Army Corps' June 2022 draft EIS puts new-work dredging at about 46 million cubic yards. A 2026 conference abstract by a University of Texas marine scientist flags larval-recruitment and brine-discharge concerns, and no permit decision was found in the sources opened.

notes.scale: Effects are centred on one channel and adjacent bays, though the entrance channel would extend roughly 10 miles into the Gulf (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: The application was filed January 3, 2019 and the draft EIS appeared in June 2022, with the issue still discussed in May 2026 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A Corps Draft Environmental Impact Statement and a FAST-41 permitting track are formal federal processes, but no decision was found (ref 1).

records.title: Houston Ship Channel Project 11 widens Galveston Bay reach, with funding gaps and habitat reuse plans
records.description: Project 11, the Houston Ship Channel Expansion, widens the Galveston Bay reach by 170 feet to 700 feet and deepens some upstream segments to 46.5 feet.
